extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, drama, and playwriting (esp. classical poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and assessing classical tragedy (Aristotelian poetics): its purpose, essential parts (plot, character, thought, diction, music, spectacle), and principles like unity, verisimilitude, and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: End/Purpose of Tragedy (refine the passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: And which by the means of Compassion and Terror, perfectly refines in us all sorts of Passions, and whatever else is like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy’s principal end is moral/affective: to 'refine' passions — not to root them out, but to curb their excess and reduce them to just moderation. This is offered as the Aristotelian answer to Plato’s objection that tragedy is dangerous to manners. The commentary explains that refinement means regulating passions so they are useful rather than vicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means to achieve the end: Terror and Compassion (catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: It excites Terror and Compassion ... it excites them by setting before our Eyes the Calamities, into which, those who are like ourselves, have fallen by involuntary Faults; and it refines them by rendering those very Misfortunes familiar to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy causes pity and fear through representation of calamities affecting characters like the audience; this emotional excitation then purges or moderates those passions (catharsis). Theatre acts as a medicine that works by pleasure — it stimulates and then relieves passions so spectators profit from observed crimes and their consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from Epic (epopeeia uses narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is to distinguish Tragedy from Epopæia, which employs only Narration, in order to obtain the same end... for what is represented to the Understanding only, does not make so deep Impressions, as that which is shewn to the Eyes of the Spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy is more immediately affecting because it enacts actions before the eyes (performance), while epic/poem-by-narration uses description and takes more time; therefore tragedy uses spectacle, acting, music for stronger immediate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot / Fable is the soul of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Composition of things, Aristotle means the Connexion, which the Causes and Incidents, that Concurr to form an Action, have with one another... I call that Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The arrangement and unity of incidents that form a single action (plot) is the most important element; a well-constituted subject/plot outranks other parts. Plot must form a coherent whole where every part contributes to the action's causes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy imitates actions, not men (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an Imitation not of Men, but of their Actions... It imitates one Action only, but it chooses the most considerable, which denotes whether a Man's Life is good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy should concentrate on a single, significant action (or compact set of causally unified incidents) rather than attempting to portray an entire life. The moral/poetic focus is the action and its consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and Recognition (revolutions and recognitions) as chief devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The most efficacious means which [tragedy] uses to affect and please, are the Peripeties and Recognizances, the Peripeties and Remembrances are inseparable parts of the Subject...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals of fortune (peripeteia) and moments of recognition are powerful mechanisms in plot to generate pity and fear; they are especially effective when integrated into the unified plot (examples: Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of importance among parts (hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six parts ... Of these six, the most considerable is the Fable... The Manners follow next... and then the Sentiments; the Diction and Music are means the Poet makes use of, and Decoration regards the Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating tragedy prioritize: (1) plot (fable), (2) character (manners), (3) thought/sentiment, (4) diction/verse, (5) music, (6) spectacle/decoration. A strong plot can outweigh weaker execution in other parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character / Manners as causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manners are that, which distinguishes those who Act... They characterize Men, and denote their Inclinations, either good or bad... they are the Causes of Good or Evil to Mankind, because they produce Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be designed so their dispositions, habits, and inclinations plausibly cause the actions of the plot. Characterization should make motives intelligible and credible; characters are secondary to plot but necessary to produce believable actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought / Sentiments (what characters say and think)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments are Discourses, by which every Action is made known, or discover their Inclinations thoughts... The Sentiments are the Faculty of expressing those things which belong to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought or 'sentiment' comprises the speeches/ideas that explain motives and the subject; it must be true to the subject and demonstrate verisimilitude. Sentiments follow naturally from character and serve to make the action intelligible; rhetoric and art can embellish them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Discourse (elocution) relies on rhetoric and common use
rubrics_metrics.description: All that has respect to Discourse, depends on Rhetorick, or the common use... the ordinary language of the People; whereas the Artful seeks to speak with Art and Method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should suit the characters and the subject: sometimes plain common speech is appropriate, sometimes elevated rhetorical style is required. Use rhetorical art to beautify discourse where fitting, but maintain suitability to character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and Chorus as means (historical necessity but subordinate)
rubrics_metrics.description: One which regards the Means... the Music. The first thing we ought to take notice of, is that Aristotle puts Music and Verse among the necessary;... Music and Dancing were looked on as a part of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music (melody) and chorus were historically integral (dance/song aligned with passion), and can intensify emotional effect; however, music serves the plot and passions and is subordinate to the fable and characters. It can be used or omitted depending on style/tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration / Spectacle is expressive but not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The Decoration of the Scenes is in some sort a part of Tragedy... but as Tragedy will bear reading without being Acted, it follows that the Decoration is not one of its Essential Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenic elements and costumes help express the nature of what is represented and contribute to effect, but they are external aids rather than constitutive of tragedy. A play can still be a tragedy without elaborate spectacle; evaluate spectacle as subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude / Probability (truth to subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments Truth, follow the Truth, when we speak those things which are necessary to the Subject; and Verisimilitude, when we say those things which are agreeable to it... at least Verisimilitude must be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech, thought, and events must be credible within the world and subject of the play. Even implausible events must behave according to internal probabilities; maintain truthfulness or likely behaviour appropriate to the characters and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and primacy of the subject (craft of constituting a subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Subject well managed, though the Manners be ill express'd, the Elocution dull, and the Sentiments mean, shall succeed better than a Piece where the Subject shall not be rightly disposed... the difficulty found in disposing the Subject is incontestable proof that the Subject is the most important and proper part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composing a unified, well-constructed subject/plot is the hardest and most crucial task for a tragedian. Evaluate a work first on whether the subject is well constituted and the incidents properly connected; plot defects typically outweigh stylistic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement explained: moderation not eradication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Peripatetics ... by To Refine the Passions, to Curb the Excess, by which they err'd, and to reduce them to a Just Moderation. And this is the End, they attribute to Tragedy, as the only one it can attain to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the moral/affective function of tragedy, look for its capacity to correct excesses — to moderate appetites, fears, ambitions — rather than to eliminate passions entirely. The aesthetic effect should teach prudence and measured feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement/order in composition (analogy to painting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the finest Colours were mixt on a Nail, confusedly, and without order, it would not give so much Pleasure as the simple Sketches of a Painter... The Poet begins by disposing the Subject and all the Parts of the Action; and afterwards adds those Manners which are proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositional order matters: organize the action and its parts before elaborating character, diction, or ornament. Like a painter sketching forms before applying color, the playwright must first structure the plot clearly, then add details and stylistic elements in service of that structure.
